newsitem.title: CHINA: China slams U.S. Congress for meddling in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China slams U.S. Congress for meddling in Hong Kong.

text.p: Beijing on Thursday accused U.S. congressmen of ignorant and arrogant meddling in Hong Kong, saying some Washington lawmakers used concerns over the territory's post-colonial future to try to contain China.

A bill approved by the U.S. House of Representatives calling on Beijing to honour its promises on Hong Kong after the territory returns to Chinese rule on July 1 was pointless, unjustified and wrong, the People's Daily said.
"This once again reveals the ugly mentality of some members of the U.S. Congress who want to lord it over the world," said the newspaper, mouthpiece of China's ruling Communist Party.
"No sovereign government could tolerate the practice of the supercilious U.S. Congress in grossly interfering in its internal affairs," it said.
Some U.S. congressmen were trying to use the Hong Kong issue to aid a policy of containment against China, it said.

The People's Daily commentary was the latest diplomatic broadside to ruffle a Sino-U.S. rapprochement that both sides say should be bolstered by a visit to Beijing next week by U.S. Vice President Al Gore.

China has promised to treat Gore well but has not held back from propaganda jabs at Washington over issues including Hong Kong, human rights and U.S. accusations that Beijing tried to channel funds to the Democratic Party.
Ill-informed U.S. congressmen had been too ready to believe vicious attacks on China's Hong Kong policy from Britain and democracy activists in the territory, the People's Daily said.
"Some U.S. news media have also fanned the flames and are eager to see Hong Kong devolve into chaos," it said.

Analysts say Hong Kong is likely to become one of the thorniest diplomatic issues in the Sino-U.S. relationship as the handover nears -- a view bolstered by Beijing's angry reaction to the recent U.S. bill.

The bill, passed by the House of Representatives' in a 416-1 vote on March 11, called on China to honour its treaty obligations, saying failure to ensure an elected legislature for Hong Kong would violate a Sino-British 1984 agreement.

China has vowed to scrap Hong Kong's current elected legislature and replace it with a Beijing-appointed body, and also plans to roll back legislation introduced by Britain to protect civil rights in the territory.
Gore is scheduled to discuss Hong Kong's future this month when he becomes the most senior U.S. official to visit China in eight years.

Gore's meetings in the Chinese capital are intended to pave the way for an exchange of presidential visits, but the new disputes over Hong Kong and campaign financing are seen by some in Washington as an obstacle to improving ties.
U.S. congressmen should keep their nation's fundamental interests in mind and not be so hasty to attack China over Hong Kong, the People's Daily warned.

"Some members of Congress, please don't be so ready with such indiscreet criticism. Why can't you study the situation and learn something about the reality of Hong Kong before you reach a conclusion?" the newspaper said.
